em_1_minuto.titulo: What if the tumor has two mutations?
em_1_minuto.texto: Mutations in the TP53 gene are common in lung cancer and usually signal a worse course. It was not known what happens when they appear together with EGFR mutations in Brazilian patients.

em_1_minuto.titulo: They read the DNA of 70 tumors
em_1_minuto.texto: Tumors from 70 operated patients were sequenced for the EGFR and TP53 genes, and the patients were followed for years.

em_1_minuto.titulo: TP53 tends to make things worse
em_1_minuto.texto: Almost half of the tumors with mutated EGFR also had mutated TP53. With mutated TP53, median survival was 59 months; without the mutation, 95 months.

em_1_minuto.titulo: Looking at TP53 in genetic testing
em_1_minuto.texto: Routine TP53 testing could help predict the course of the disease and the response to treatment. The study also recalls the R337H variant, very common in Brazil.

secoes.lede: EGFR and TP53 play opposite roles in cell growth, and both can fail in the same tumor.

itens.texto: Gene for a receptor that tells the cell to grow. When mutated, it stays “switched on” all the time. There are targeted drugs against it, such as erlotinib.
Tumor suppressor gene on chromosome 17. It helps repair DNA, stop cell division and eliminate damaged cells. There is still no approved drug that corrects it in lung cancer.

blocos.html:
Lung cancer was the leading cause of cancer death worldwide in 2020. The most common type, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), accounts for 85% to 90% of cases. Drugs against EGFR have greatly improved treatment, but about 30% of patients do not respond from the start. One suspect is co-mutations, and the most frequent of them is in TP53.

The frequency of EGFR mutations varies with ancestry: about 60% in Asians and 20% in Europeans. In Brazil, it ranges from 19% in the South to 22%–30% in the Southeast. There were no data on the EGFR + TP53 combination in Brazilians.

secoes.titulo: From frozen tumor to DNA reading
secoes.lede: A study that combined pathology, sequencing and bioinformatics.

itens.texto: 70 fresh-frozen tumors, removed in surgeries from 2003 to 2010 at the A.C. Camargo Cancer Center in São Paulo. Freezing avoids reading errors that formalin can cause in DNA.
Two experienced pathologists confirmed the diagnosis using the 2021 WHO classification: 46 non-squamous and 24 squamous tumors.
DNA was extracted and the EGFR and TP53 genes were read by next-generation sequencing (Illumina MiSeq), with each stretch read at least 100 times.

Reads were aligned to the human reference genome (BWA), variants were identified (GATK) and annotated (VEP, dbSNP, COSMIC and ClinVar), with filters to separate tumor mutations from inherited variants.
Survival was analyzed with Kaplan-Meier curves and Cox models, taking into account stage, relapse, treatment and mutations.

blocos.html: To avoid false positives, only mutations seen in at least 10 reads, with a minimum frequency of 5% in the tumor and rare in the population (under 0.1% in the 1000 Genomes and ExAC databases), were counted.

secoes.lede: See how many tumors had each mutation and how this related to survival.

parametros.leitura: 29 tumors had mutated TP53 and 23 had mutated EGFR. Ten had both: 14.3% of the total, but 43.5% of those with mutated EGFR.
With mutated TP53, median survival dropped from 95 to 59 months. The difference was at the edge of statistical significance (p = 0.079).
Tumor stage after surgery was the clearest factor: in the more advanced stages, median survival was cut in half (p = 0.028).

blocos.nota: Percentages and median survival from the text, Table 1 and Figure 1 of the paper.

itens.texto: 44 men and 21 women, with a median age of 65 (range 41 to 96). Most of European ancestry, according to medical records.
Over about 4 years of follow-up (median), 54.3% died. There was local relapse in 17.4% and distant metastasis in 17.4%, mostly in the brain and bones.
Most were missense and classified as pathogenic. The most repeated one, p.Gly245Cys, appeared in 3 patients.

blocos.html: In the model combining several factors, the highest risk of death (p = 0.029) brought together: stage IIIA–IIIB, relapse with distant metastasis, lack of response to platinum chemotherapy and to erlotinib, uncommon EGFR mutations, mutated TP53 and the EGFR + TP53 co-mutation.

secoes.titulo: An admixed population, and a very Brazilian variant
secoes.lede: The mix of ancestries may change the mutation profile of tumors.

blocos.html:
The Brazilian population is one of the most genetically diverse in the world, the result of five centuries of mixing among Asian, European, African and Indigenous peoples. In this group, the rate of TP53 mutations was about half of that described in other studies: 21.4% in non-squamous tumors and 20% in squamous ones, versus 40% and 51% in the literature.

The EGFR + TP53 co-mutation (43.5%), however, was within the range reported in other countries (17% to 72%). Another study, by Labbé and colleagues, found no effect of the co-mutation on survival in early stages, which shows the question is still open.

The authors note that Li-Fraumeni syndrome, caused by the R337H variant in TP53, is rare worldwide but very frequent in Brazil. Finding this variant in a tumor's genetic profile should raise suspicion of the syndrome. One patient in this study had the variant, but no EGFR mutation. See the full study on R337H →

blocos.titulo: Limitations pointed out by the authors
itens: The group is small: only 10 patients had the EGFR + TP53 co-mutation.
The study is descriptive and exploratory; the findings need to be confirmed in larger groups.
Ancestry came from medical records, not from genetic ancestry tests.

secoes.titulo: What the study allows us to say
secoes.lede: A warning about TP53 that still needs to be confirmed.

blocos.html: The study suggests that TP53 mutation tends to worsen survival and may signal a poorer response to platinum chemotherapy and erlotinib in patients with EGFR-mutated NSCLC operated on at an early stage. According to the authors, including TP53 in routine genetic testing would help clarify its role, alone or together with other mutations.

glossario.def: Non-small cell lung cancer, the most common type of lung cancer.
Gene for a receptor that stimulates cell growth. When mutated, it can drive the tumor.
The “guardian of the genome” gene, which makes the p53 protein, responsible for stopping cells with damaged DNA.
When two mutations appear together in the same tumor.
A change in one DNA letter that swaps an amino acid in the protein.
Technique that reads millions of DNA stretches at the same time.
Use of computers and databases to analyze biological information, such as DNA sequences.
A DNA change whose effect on health is not yet known.
Sample frozen right after surgery. It preserves DNA better than a formalin-fixed paraffin block.
Step-shaped graph showing the percentage of patients alive over time.
Statistical analysis that measures the effect of several factors at once on the risk of death.
Classification of the size and spread of the cancer. Stage III is more advanced than stages I and II.
Inherited syndrome that raises the risk of several cancers, caused by variants in TP53, such as R337H.
